query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing serrated (i.e., roughened and tortuous) phase boundaries in the lamellar colonies of eutectic HEAs via a tailored thermo‐mechanical processing step will simultaneously enhance room-temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to alloys with conventional, smooth lamellar interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast or conventionally processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual-phase lamellar (L12 + B2) colonies with smooth, straight phase boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation and propagation under tensile loading at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment (for example, a combination of warm rolling at a selected temperature followed by a short annealing step) designed to modify the morphology of the phase boundaries so that they become serrated.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation of eutectic HEAs with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure similar to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, processed under conditions that do not substantially alter the phase fractions or lamellar spacing aside from inducing interface serrations.
generation.structural_mediator: The newly induced serrated phase boundaries serve as crack deflectors and local strain hardening sites, thereby improving damage tolerance and enhancing back-stress effects across the lamellae.
generation.mechanism: Serrated boundaries increase the tortuosity of potential crack paths, which delays microcrack initiation and inhibits their coalescence. In addition, these irregular interfaces can enhance internal load partitioning and promote work hardening (via augmented back stresses), allowing the alloy to sustain higher stresses and larger uniform plastic deformation before catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline eutectic HEA with smooth boundaries, the alloy exhibiting serrated phase boundaries will demonstrate an increased yield strength and ultimate tensile strength together with a higher tensile elongation at failure under room-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with conventional lamellar colonies that possess smooth, straight phase boundaries which facilitate early microcrack initiation and propagation, leading to the well-known strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only in eutectic HEAs where the microstructure consists of dual-phase lamellae (e.g., L12 and B2 phases) and where the processing parameters can be tuned to modify interface morphology without disrupting phase fractions or overall lamellar spacing. Its effectiveness in alloys with different architectures or in significantly different processing regimes remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of improvement in strength and ductility as well as the optimal processing parameters for generating the ideal serrated interface morphology are not fully defined; additional studies are needed to quantify the back-stress contributions and verify that no adverse phase transformations occur during processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples. Process one set via conventional thermo-mechanical treatment to yield typical smooth lamellar colonies (baseline). Process the second set with the tailored treatment (warm rolling plus annealing) to intentionally produce serrated phase boundaries. Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets while concurrently conducting microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM or in situ microscopy) to assess boundary morphology and crack initiation behavior.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Fractographic analysis to evaluate crack initiation sites and paths
Quantitative characterization of boundary serration (e.g., amplitude, spacing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with induced serrated phase boundaries do not show a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline samples, or if fractography/microscopy shows no retardation or alteration of microcrack initiation/propagation mechanisms, then the hypothesis is falsified.
